subject: chemistry-1
question: A hypothetical teaching solution contains 0.02 mol of KCl dissolved per liter of water. Assuming complete dissociation, what is the concentration of K+ expressed in mEq/L?

options.text: 2 mEq/L, because the amount in moles is divided by the charge on the potassium ion
20 mEq/L, because 0.02 mol/L equals 20 mmol/L and K+ carries a single positive charge
40 mEq/L, because the K+ and the Cl- released by each formula unit are both counted
0.02 mEq/L, because for a monovalent ion the equivalent concentration equals the molarity

explanation:
Two steps are required. Convert the unit prefix: 0.02 mol/L x 1000 = 20 mmol/L. Then multiply by the charge magnitude of 1 for K+, giving 20 mEq/L. Option D correctly notes that mmol/L and mEq/L coincide for monovalent ions but fails to convert mol/L to mmol/L first. Chloride is a distinct anion reported separately and is never folded into the potassium result.

ELI-10: Work the prefix and the charge as separate operations. The prefix: a millimole is one thousandth of a mole, so 0.02 mol/L becomes 20 mmol/L by multiplying by 1000. The charge: potassium is K+, one unit of charge, so multiplying by 1 leaves the value at 20 mEq/L. The equality of mmol/L and mEq/L for monovalent ions is a useful check, but it holds only after the amounts are in the same prefix - 0.02 and 20 are not interchangeable.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)
